title: Judges 13:21–25
context: After the angel’s departure, Manoah realizes who the visitor was and fears death for having seen God, while his wife reasons from God’s acceptance of their offering that he means them good. Samson is born, the LORD blesses him, and the Spirit begins to stir him. Arminian and Reformed readers share this passage as a picture of reverent fear, wise faith, and God’s faithfulness to his promise, while recognizing that the Spirit’s empowerment does not make Samson’s later choices automatically faithful.

verses.text: But the LORD’s angel didn’t appear to Manoah or to his wife any more. Then Manoah knew that he was the LORD’s angel.
verses.arminianNotes:
The angel does not appear again, and Manoah knows he was the LORD’s angel. Recognition comes after the encounter.

Arminian readers see understanding growing through experience and reflection. Manoah comes to see what had been in front of him all along.
verses.reformedNotes:
Only after the visitor departs does Manoah grasp who he was. The narrative highlights the delayed realization.

Reformed readers see God revealing himself in his own time. Both traditions read this as shared ground, and both note that the text identifies him as the LORD’s angel without further explanation.

verses.text: Manoah said to his wife, “We shall surely die, because we have seen God.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Manoah says, “We shall surely die, because we have seen God.” His fear is sincere.

Arminian readers see a reverent but anxious response to God’s nearness, echoing Genesis 32:30 and Exodus 33:20.
verses.reformedNotes:
Manoah links the encounter with seeing God. Interpreters in both traditions differ on what that implies about the messenger.

Reformed readers see holy fear before divine presence. Both traditions read Manoah’s fear plainly and without settling the identity question, noting that his wife will offer a calmer reading of what has happened.

verses.text: But his wife said to him, “If the LORD were pleased to kill us, he wouldn’t have received a burnt offering and a meal offering at our hand, and he wouldn’t have shown us all these things, nor would he have told us such things as these at this time.”
verses.arminianNotes:
His wife reasons that if God wanted to kill them, he would not have accepted their offering, shown them these things, or told them such news. Her logic is sound.

Arminian readers see faith reasoning from God’s gracious acts.
verses.reformedNotes:
She reads the evidence of grace correctly. God’s acceptance and promise imply he means them good.

Reformed readers see assurance grounded in what God has done and said. Both traditions share this reading and often admire the woman’s steady faith as wise and pastoral.

verses.text: The woman bore a son and named him Samson. The child grew, and the LORD blessed him.
verses.arminianNotes:
The woman bears a son and names him Samson; the child grows, and the LORD blesses him. The promise is fulfilled.

Arminian readers see God’s blessing on the child’s early life, before Samson’s own choices shape his story.
verses.reformedNotes:
God keeps his word to the couple. Samson grows under the LORD’s blessing.

Reformed readers see God’s faithfulness in fulfilling his promise. Both traditions read this as shared ground, and Hebrews 11:32 later lists Samson among those who acted by faith.

verses.text: The LORD’s Spirit began to move him in Mahaneh Dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD’s Spirit begins to stir Samson at Mahaneh Dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol. His calling starts to take shape.

Arminian readers see the Spirit empowering Samson for his task, with Samson still responsible for how he responds.
verses.reformedNotes:
The Spirit’s stirring marks the beginning of Samson’s work. The empowering comes from God.

Reformed readers see God equipping his chosen deliverer. Both traditions agree that the Spirit’s work here is empowerment for service, and that it does not by itself guarantee a faithful life, as the following chapters show.
